version.changelog:
SmithNode 1.0.9 – Adds explicit permission and requirement metadata

- Added a [ClawHub](https://clawhub.com/smithnodebyte/smithnode) reference and link.
- Expanded the skill manifest: now lists required binaries (`git`, `cargo`, `curl`), runtime permissions (`network`, `filesystem`, `shell`), and optional environment variables for API keys.
- Documented what the skill does and does NOT require (e.g., no root or cloud accounts needed).
- Updated the README to clarify build/runtime prerequisites and permission scope for local and AI-driven validators.

llm.summary: The skill largely matches its stated purpose (running a P2P validator) but contains several inconsistencies and some scope‑creep instructions (contributor automation and external install scripts) that warrant caution before installing or running it.

dimensions.detail: The name/description (P2P validator for AI agents) aligns with the included source, runtime permissions, and optional AI API keys. However there is an inconsistency between the top-level registry summary (which listed no required binaries / only curl) and the SKILL.md / skill.json (which require git and cargo). The code bundle present (Rust source) is appropriate for a build-from-source validator.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions are explicit about building, generating a local keypair, and running a validator; those are in-scope. But the docs also include an AI contributor workflow that instructs AI agents to use the GitHub CLI (gh) to fork, push, create PRs, and even merge if permitted — that requires GitHub credentials and grants broad rights unrelated to simply running a validator. The guides also recommend running external install scripts (e.g., curl | sh for rustup and Ollama install), deploying web dashboards, and opening public RPC ports — all of which broaden the operational scope and risk surface beyond merely running a local validator.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no formal install spec in the registry (instruction-only), which reduces automatic disk writes. However the SKILL.md and other docs instruct users to run curl-based installers (rustup, Ollama) and to build from source with cargo. Those external install scripts are common but inherently carry risk if run blindly; the project also provides Docker/Kubernetes examples which are conventional.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Optional environment variables are limited to cloud AI API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, Together) which are reasonable for cloud-backed AI usage. But the contributor docs actively encourage use of GitHub CLI and automated PR workflows that would require GitHub credentials or tokens — this is unrelated to validator operation and elevates credential exposure risk if an agent follows the contributor automation. The skill does not require any unrelated system-wide secrets, and it explicitly warns to never share the validator private key, which is good.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is not always: true, does not ask to be force-included, and requests normal permissions for this type of software (network, filesystem, shell). Those privileges are proportionate for a full node/validator. Note: the docs recommend exposing RPC endpoints publicly and running services on VPS/Fly/Vercel — doing so increases external exposure but is a deployment choice rather than an inherent skill privilege.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
Summary of what to consider before installing or running this skill:

- Coherence: The code and instructions match the stated purpose (a Rust-based P2P validator). Expect to build from source with git + cargo and to give the process network/filesystem/shell access.

- Inconsistency to note: The registry summary at the top disagrees with SKILL.md/skill.json about required binaries (the docs require git and cargo). Assume git/cargo are needed.

- Credential risk: You should never share your validator private key. The contributor guides, however, encourage GitHub automation (gh CLI) which requires tokens/credentials — only give GH tokens if you explicitly want to allow contribution automation and you understand the scope of that token. Prefer human-mediated GitHub operations.

- Installation risk: The documentation suggests running external install scripts via curl | sh (rustup, Ollama). Those are common but run third-party code on your machine — audit the script or run in an isolated VM/container.

- Network exposure: Examples encourage binding RPC to 0.0.0.0 and publishing RPC endpoints. If you run a validator, prefer binding RPC to localhost and using a reverse proxy or firewall to limit exposure. Do not publish your ~/.smithnode keypair.json or make it world-readable.

- Operational safety: If you want to test, run the node in a sandboxed environment (VM or container), build from source yourself, and keep keys offline. Use Ollama (local) if you want to avoid sending prompts to cloud providers and avoid providing cloud API keys unless necessary.

- Code review: The repository includes networking and AI-client code (reqwest calls to AI provider endpoints) — if you plan to run it in production or with real credentials, review the AI client code paths and network endpoints, and consider restricting outbound connections via firewall rules.

- When in doubt: Run the build/run steps in an isolated environment, do not provide secrets (API keys or GitHub tokens) to any automated agent unless required and you trust the workflow, and prefer local AI providers for privacy.
